explanation: David resolves to muzzle his mouth ('keep my mouth with a bridle') around godless critics, determined not to let acute suffering provoke him into ungodly complaints that dishonor God. Psalm 39:1 (KJV) - "I said, I will take heed to my ways, that I sin not with my tongue: I will keep my mouth with a bridle, while the wicked is before me."

question: What internal emotional eruption occurred when David attempted to suppress his grief in Psalm 39:2-3?
opt1: His tears dried up like summer dust, his bones broke with fever, and he fell into a deep trance
opt2: He was dumb with silence, holding peace even from good; his sorrow was stirred, heart was hot, the fire burned while musing, then he spoke
opt3: His tongue cleaveth to his jaw, his eyes failed with looking upward, and his friends wept around him
opt4: His spirit departed from his flesh, his crown fell into the dust, and he tore his royal garments
correct: He was dumb with silence, holding peace even from good; his sorrow was stirred, heart was hot, the fire burned while musing, then he spoke
explanation: Repressed grief intensified: total silence backfired, causing inner sorrow to boil like an unvented subterranean fire until the pressure burst forth in speech. Psalm 39:2-3 (KJV) - "I was dumb with silence, I held my peace, even from good; and my sorrow was stirred. My heart was hot within me, while I was musing the fire burned: then spake I with my tongue,"

question: What sobering perspective on mortality and human frailty does David ask God to teach him in Psalm 39:4?
opt1: "O God, reveal unto me the number of my years; that I may prepare a sepulchre on Mount Zion;"
opt2: "Lord, show me the day of my death; that I may set my house in order and anoint my son king;"
opt3: "LORD, make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is; that I may know how frail I am."
opt4: "Almighty, teach me the secrets of the grave; that my soul may not be terrified before the pit;"
correct: "LORD, make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is; that I may know how frail I am."
explanation: David prays for realistic self-awareness: wanting to comprehend the brevity of his lifespan and his utter creaturely frailty from God's vantage point. Psalm 39:4 (KJV) - "LORD, make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is; that I may know how frail I am."

question: What brief anatomical measurement and universal verdict on human existence are given in Psalm 39:5?
opt1: "Behold, my life is as a fleeing shadow, and my strength as a crushed moth: verily all kings are but dust. Selah;"
opt2: "Lo, thou hast measured my days with a span, and my years as a drop in the ocean: surely flesh is as withered grass. Selah;"
opt3: "Thou hast made my days like a weaver's shuttle, and my life as an empty vapor: truly mortal man is as vanity. Selah;"
opt4: "Behold, thou hast made my days as an handbreadth; and mine age is as nothing before thee: verily every man at his best state is altogether vanity. Selah."
correct: "Behold, thou hast made my days as an handbreadth; and mine age is as nothing before thee: verily every man at his best state is altogether vanity. Selah."
explanation: Lifespan is measured by the width of four fingers ('handbreadth'); before God's eternity, human life is virtually zero, and even humanity at its absolute peak ('at his best state') is mere vapor ('hebel' - vanity). Psalm 39:5 (KJV) - "Behold, thou hast made my days as an handbreadth; and mine age is as nothing before thee: verily every man at his best state is altogether vanity. Selah."

question: What two futile pursuits of worldly men are rebuked in Psalm 39:6?
opt1: Walking in a vain shew (a phantom shadow), being disquieted in vain, and heaping up riches without knowing who shall gather them
opt2: Building towers of stone that crumble in earthquakes, and buying chariots of iron that rust in rain
opt3: Seeking foreign alliances that fail in war, and writing books of philosophy that confound the simple
opt4: Planting vineyards that strangers harvest, and fighting for crowns that perish in a single generation
correct: Walking in a vain shew (a phantom shadow), being disquieted in vain, and heaping up riches without knowing who shall gather them
explanation: Mortal bustle is a phantom parade ('walketh in a vain shew'): people torment themselves chasing illusions, frantically amassing wealth with zero knowledge of who will inherit it. Psalm 39:6 (KJV) - "Surely every man walketh in a vain shew: surely they are disquieted in vain: he heapeth up riches, and knoweth not who shall gather them."

question: With what foundational pivot of detachment from earthly vanity does David turn to God in Psalm 39:7?
opt1: "Wherefore, O God, shall I despair? my fortress is upon Mount Zion;"
opt2: "And now, Lord, what wait I for? my hope is in thee."
opt3: "Therefore, O King, will I offer sacrifice: my trust is in the blood of the altar;"
opt4: "Behold, O Almighty, I look unto the hills: my help cometh from the heavens;"
correct: "And now, Lord, what wait I for? my hope is in thee."
explanation: Recognizing the bankruptcy of worldly pursuits, David disengages from earthly expectations and re-anchors his total hope exclusively in Yahweh. Psalm 39:7 (KJV) - "And now, Lord, what wait I for? my hope is in thee."

question: What submission to divine sovereignty explains David's reverent silence in Psalm 39:9?
opt1: "I held my peace before the assembly; because the prophet commanded me;"
opt2: "I bowed my head in sackcloth; because my iniquity was great;"
opt3: "I was dumb, I opened not my mouth; because thou didst it."
opt4: "I sat in silence by the waters of Babylon; because our sanctuary was burned;"
correct: "I was dumb, I opened not my mouth; because thou didst it."
explanation: The ultimate posture of submissive faith: recognizing that his affliction was orchestrated by God's sovereign, purposeful hand ('because thou didst it'), David ceases all complaining. Psalm 39:9 (KJV) - "I was dumb, I opened not my mouth; because thou didst it."

question: To what fragile insect's destructive work is the consumption of human beauty compared in Psalm 39:11?
opt1: Thou consumest his strength like a locust devouring green fields
opt2: Thou crushest his bones like a grasshopper trodden in the dust
opt3: Thou scatterest his riches like spider's webs blown by the east wind
opt4: Thou makest his beauty to consume away like a moth
correct: Thou makest his beauty to consume away like a moth
explanation: When God disciplines man for iniquity, human physical beauty and pride disintegrate as quietly and thoroughly as expensive garments eaten away by moths. Psalm 39:11 (KJV) - "When thou with rebukes dost correct man for iniquity, thou makest his beauty to consume away like a moth: surely every man is vanity. Selah."

question: What pilgrim status before God does David claim when pleading for his tears to be heard in Psalm 39:12?
opt1: "For I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner, as all my fathers were."
opt2: "For I am the anointed king of Israel, and the sweet psalmist of Judah;"
opt3: "For I am a servant in thy sanctuary, and a keeper of the holy ark;"
opt4: "For I am a son of the covenant, and a warrior of the twelve tribes;"
correct: "For I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner, as all my fathers were."
explanation: Like Abraham and the patriarchs, David identifies himself as a resident alien ('stranger and sojourner') on earth, dependent entirely on God's hospitable protection. Psalm 39:12 (KJV) - "Hear my prayer, O LORD, and give ear unto my cry; hold not thy peace at my tears: for I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner, as all my fathers were."

question: Who was 'Jeduthun' mentioned in the superscription of Psalm 39?
opt1: A Benjamite captain who carried David's royal shield in battle
opt2: One of the three chief directors of temple music appointed by David, alongside Asaph and Heman
opt3: A prophet from Shiloh who rebuked the princes of Judah for usury
opt4: A high priest who preserved the ark during the Absalom rebellion
correct: One of the three chief directors of temple music appointed by David, alongside Asaph and Heman
explanation: Jeduthun (also called Ethan, 1 Chron 16:41-42, 25:1-6) was one of David's three master musicians who led prophetic praise in the tabernacle liturgy. Psalm 39:Title (KJV) - "To the chief Musician, even to Jeduthun, A Psalm of David."

question: What dramatic rescue from a deadly quagmire does David celebrate in Psalm 40:1-2?
opt1: He offered sacrifices at Zion; God sent an angel, plucked him from the net of Saul, and led him into a fortified city
opt2: He waited patiently for the LORD; God inclined, heard his cry, brought him up out of an horrible pit and miry clay, set his feet upon a rock, and established his goings
opt3: He fasted forty days; God divided the river Jordan, carried him across the deep waters, and built him a house of cedar
opt4: He cried aloud in the cave; God struck his enemies with blindness, broke their bronze chariots, and crowned him king
correct: He waited patiently for the LORD; God inclined, heard his cry, brought him up out of an horrible pit and miry clay, set his feet upon a rock, and established his goings
explanation: A classic salvation testimony: patient waiting rewarded by divine rescue from a subterranean muddy dungeon ('horrible pit and miry clay') onto solid rock stability. Psalm 40:1-2 (KJV) - "I waited patiently for the LORD; and he inclined unto me, and heard my cry. He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings."

question: What evangelistic fruit and corporate reaction result from David's 'new song' in Psalm 40:3?
opt1: "And the Levites sang with harps in the sanctuary: and all the tribes of Israel brought tithes of gold;"
opt2: "And my enemies were terrified before my face: and the kings of the heathen surrendered their crowns;"
opt3: "And he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God: many shall see it, and fear, and shall trust in the LORD."
opt4: "And the angels of heaven rejoiced in the presence of God: and the congregation shouted for joy;"
correct: "And he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God: many shall see it, and fear, and shall trust in the LORD."
explanation: Salvation produces authentic witness: God places a fresh hymn of praise in the mouth, which spectators see and revere, leading many to trust in Yahweh. Psalm 40:3 (KJV) - "And he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God: many shall see it, and fear, and shall trust in the LORD."

question: How does David describe the sheer, unreckonable multitude of God's wonderful works and thoughts toward us in Psalm 40:5?
opt1: "They are higher than the stars of heaven: if I would measure them, they exceed the sands of the sea;"
opt2: "They are deeper than the great abyss: if I would write them in a scroll, the earth could not contain them;"
opt3: "They are greater than all the gold of Ophir: if I would weigh them, the balance of the sanctuary would break;"
opt4: "They cannot be reckoned up in order unto thee: if I would declare and speak of them, they are more than can be numbered."
correct: "They cannot be reckoned up in order unto thee: if I would declare and speak of them, they are more than can be numbered."
explanation: God's providential miracles and loving thoughts toward His people defy all human calculation, surpassing all ability to count or enumerate. Psalm 40:5 (KJV) - "Many, O LORD my God, are thy wonderful works which thou hast done, and thy thoughts which are to us-ward: they cannot be reckoned up in order unto thee: if I would declare and speak of them, they are more than can be numbered."

question: What profound theological truth regarding animal sacrifice and obedience is declared in Psalm 40:6?
opt1: "Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened: burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required."
opt2: "The blood of bulls and goats hath washed away my sin; mine eyes hast thou opened to see thy salvation;"
opt3: "Burnt sacrifices of seven rams are comely for the sanctuary; my hands hast thou washed in innocency;"
opt4: "Tithes of wheat and oil are pleasing to the Lord; my heart hast thou filled with understanding;"
correct: "Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened: burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required."
explanation: Cited in Hebrews 10:5-6: God takes no ultimate pleasure in mechanical animal blood rituals; He desires responsive, consecrated obedience ('mine ears hast thou opened/dug'). Psalm 40:6 (KJV) - "Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened: burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required."

question: What supreme Messianic declaration of voluntary incarnation and obedience to God's will is recorded in Psalm 40:7-8?
opt1: "Then said I, Behold, I bring an offering: in the tables of stone it is commanded, I will keep thy statutes forever;"
opt2: "Then said I, Lo, I come: in the volume of the book it is written of me, I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is within my heart."
opt3: "Then cried I, Establish my throne: in the covenant of David it is promised, I will reign in righteousness;"
opt4: "Then prayed I, Forgive my transgression: in the law of Moses it is written, The Lord will have mercy upon Israel;"
correct: "Then said I, Lo, I come: in the volume of the book it is written of me, I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is within my heart."
explanation: Applied directly to Jesus Christ in Hebrews 10:7-9: Christ stepped into human history declaring 'Lo, I come', fulfilling the entire prophetic scroll ('volume of the book') through perfect delight in doing the Father's will. Psalm 40:7-8 (KJV) - "Then said I, Lo, I come: in the volume of the book it is written of me, I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is within my heart."

question: How did David boldly declare God's character in the great congregation in Psalm 40:9-10?
opt1: Recited the genealogies of Judah, blew the silver trumpets, and pronounced the curses of Mount Ebal
opt2: Collected tithes of silver, displayed the sword of Goliath, and read the laws of the tabernacle
opt3: Preached righteousness, refrained not lips, hid not righteousness in heart, declared faithfulness, salvation, lovingkindness, and truth
opt4: Anointed the elders with holy oil, offered a thousand bullocks, and kept silence for seven days
correct: Preached righteousness, refrained not lips, hid not righteousness in heart, declared faithfulness, salvation, lovingkindness, and truth
explanation: Five divine attributes proclaimed publicly without compromise: righteousness, faithfulness, salvation, lovingkindness, and truth in the assembly of worshipers. Psalm 40:9-10 (KJV) - "I have preached righteousness in the great congregation: lo, I have not refrained my lips, O LORD, thou knowest. I have not hid thy righteousness within my heart; I have declared thy faithfulness and thy salvation: I have not concealed thy lovingkindness and thy truth from the great congregation."

question: What crushing number of iniquities and physical disorientation does David confess in Psalm 40:12?
opt1: Sins heavier than the stones of the valley, striking his bones so that he cannot stand before the altar
opt2: Transgressions deeper than the subterranean waters, blinding his eyes so that he cannot see the sun
opt3: Faults burning like a furnace of fire, consuming his flesh so that his tongue cleaveth to his mouth
opt4: Iniquities more than the hairs of his head, taking hold of him so that he is not able to look up, and his heart fails him
correct: Iniquities more than the hairs of his head, taking hold of him so that he is not able to look up, and his heart fails him
explanation: Consciousness of sin overwhelms him: his iniquities exceed the hairs of his head, paralyzing him with shame so that he cannot look up, causing his heart to fail. Psalm 40:12 (KJV) - "For innumerable evils have compassed me about: mine iniquities have taken hold upon me, so that I am not able to look up; they are more than the hairs of mine head: therefore my heart faileth me."

question: What separate psalm in Book 2 of the Psalter is virtually identical to Psalm 40:13-17?
opt1: Psalm 70 (a liturgical excerpt designed 'to bring to remembrance')
opt2: Psalm 53 (a duplicate of Psalm 14)
opt3: Psalm 108 (a composite of Psalms 57 and 60)
opt4: Psalm 144 (an adaptation of Psalm 18)
correct: Psalm 70 (a liturgical excerpt designed 'to bring to remembrance')
explanation: The urgent petition of Psalm 40:13-17 ('Be pleased, O LORD, to deliver me: O LORD, make haste to help me') was excerpted and reused as standalone Psalm 70. Psalm 40:13 (KJV) - "Be pleased, O LORD, to deliver me: O LORD, make haste to help me."

question: What taunt of malicious mockers does David pray will be turned back upon themselves in Psalm 40:15?
opt1: "Let them be scattered like chaff that shout unto me, Where is thy king;"
opt2: "Let them be desolate for a reward of their shame that say unto me, Aha, aha."
opt3: "Let them fall into their own pit that whisper against me, He shall rise no more;"
opt4: "Let their lips be struck with silence that cry unto me, Behold his sorrow;"
correct: "Let them be desolate for a reward of their shame that say unto me, Aha, aha."
explanation: The enemies sneer with gloating contempt ('Aha, aha'); David prays their malicious celebration will rebound into shocking desolation and shame. Psalm 40:15 (KJV) - "Let them be desolate for a reward of their shame that say unto me, Aha, aha."

question: With what comforting contrast between his poverty and God's active mindfulness does Psalm 40 conclude in verse 17?
opt1: "For I am the anointed king of Judah; and the Lord hath established my throne: praise ye the Lord;"
opt2: "Though my strength faileth; yet the angel of the Lord encampeth around my tent: Amen and Amen;"
opt3: "But I am poor and needy; yet the Lord thinketh upon me: thou art my help and my deliverer; make no tarrying, O my God."
opt4: "Behold, I am a stranger in the earth; yet the Almighty will give me an everlasting kingdom;"
correct: "But I am poor and needy; yet the Lord thinketh upon me: thou art my help and my deliverer; make no tarrying, O my God."
explanation: A breathtaking truth of personal providence: though the believer is completely destitute ('poor and needy'), the infinite Lord is actively, constantly thinking upon him. Psalm 40:17 (KJV) - "But I am poor and needy; yet the Lord thinketh upon me: thou art my help and my deliverer; make no tarrying, O my God."

question: What beatitude of divine preservation and deliverance opens Psalm 41:1?
opt1: "Blessed is the king that judgeth with equity: the Lord will establish his throne forever;"
opt2: "Blessed are they that dwell in the house of the Lord: they will be still praising thee;"
opt3: "Blessed is he that considereth the poor: the LORD will deliver him in time of trouble."
opt4: "Blessed is the man whose transgression is forgiven: the Lord will cover all his iniquities;"
correct: "Blessed is he that considereth the poor: the LORD will deliver him in time of trouble."
explanation: God pronounces special beatitude upon those who show considerate, active compassion toward the weak and impoverished ('the poor'), promising rescue in their own crises. Psalm 41:1 (KJV) - "Blessed is he that considereth the poor: the LORD will deliver him in time of trouble."

question: What tender nursing care and bedside healing does the LORD provide during sickness in Psalm 41:3?
opt1: "The Lord will send His prophet with sweet balm: He will quench the burning fever before dawn;"
opt2: "The Almighty will anoint his head with oil: He will give him water from the sanctuary spring;"
opt3: "God will command his bones to be healed: He will clothe him with garments of health and strength;"
opt4: "The LORD will strengthen him upon the bed of languishing: thou wilt make all his bed in his sickness."
correct: "The LORD will strengthen him upon the bed of languishing: thou wilt make all his bed in his sickness."
explanation: Touching domestic imagery of God as a tender bedside nurse: Yahweh sustains the weakened patient on his sickbed and smooths ('makes') his bed during illness. Psalm 41:3 (KJV) - "The LORD will strengthen him upon the bed of languishing: thou wilt make all his bed in his sickness."

question: What heartless, impatient wish do David's enemies whisper concerning his impending death in Psalm 41:5?
opt1: "Mine enemies speak evil of me, When shall he die, and his name perish?"
opt2: "Behold, his strength is broken: let us seize his crown before his son can reign;"
opt3: "The curse of God hath overtaken him: let his palaces be burned with fire;"
opt4: "His sin hath found him out: let his memory be blotted from the gates of Zion;"
correct: "Mine enemies speak evil of me, When shall he die, and his name perish?"
explanation: Cruel malice: instead of showing sympathy, adversaries eagerly anticipate his demise, asking how soon he will die so that his very name and legacy will perish. Psalm 41:5 (KJV) - "Mine enemies speak evil of me, When shall he die, and his name perish?"

question: How does the treacherous visitor behave when coming to inspect David on his sickbed in Psalm 41:6?
opt1: Brings poisoned wine, sprinkles bitter herbs upon the floor, and laughs before the servants
opt2: Speaks vanity, his heart gathers iniquity to itself, and when he goeth abroad, he telleth it
opt3: Pretends to offer prayers, steals the royal signet ring, and reports his weakness to the Philistines
opt4: Wears sackcloth in the chamber, but throws dust upon the roof, and conspires with Absalom
correct: Speaks vanity, his heart gathers iniquity to itself, and when he goeth abroad, he telleth it
explanation: A master portrait of duplicity: a hypocritical visitor feigns concern, secretly gathers intelligence on David's failing health, and immediately gossips and plots slander outside. Psalm 41:6 (KJV) - "And if he come to see me, he speaketh vanity: his heart gathereth iniquity to itself; when he goeth abroad, he telleth it."

question: What famous prophecy of intimate betrayal, quoted by Jesus of Judas Iscariot, is found in Psalm 41:9?
opt1: "My companion in the sanctuary, with whom I took sweet counsel, hath drawn his sword against my life;"
opt2: "The counselor of my right hand, who shared my royal table, hath sold my kingdom for thirty pieces of silver;"
opt3: "Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me."
opt4: "My brother who was nursed at my mother's breast, hath joined the host of my persecutors;"
correct: "Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me."
explanation: Fulfilled in Ahithophel's betrayal of David (2 Sam 15) and quoted directly by Jesus of Judas at the Last Supper (John 13:18): table fellowship was sacred; kicking one's host was heinous treachery. Psalm 41:9 (KJV) - "Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me."

question: What objective evidence reassures David of God's continuing favor in Psalm 41:11?
opt1: "Because my health is restored, and my hair is black like a raven;"
opt2: "Because my storehouses are filled with wheat, and my vats overflow with new wine;"
opt3: "Because the high priest hath blessed my house, and the ark abideth in Zion;"
opt4: "By this I know that thou favourest me, because mine enemy doth not triumph over me."
correct: "By this I know that thou favourest me, because mine enemy doth not triumph over me."
explanation: The ultimate proof of divine favor: despite extensive plotting, the adversary was prevented from shouting the final victory shout over David. Psalm 41:11 (KJV) - "By this I know that thou favourest me, because mine enemy doth not triumph over me."

question: What permanent relational standing does God grant David in his integrity in Psalm 41:12?
opt1: "And as for me, thou upholdest me in mine integrity, and settest me before thy face for ever."
opt2: "Thou crownest me with an incorruptible crown, and establishest my kingdom in peace;"
opt3: "Thou clothest me with garments of light, and makest my memory glorious in Israel;"
opt4: "Thou leadest me beside the still waters, and givest me an eternal inheritance;"
correct: "And as for me, thou upholdest me in mine integrity, and settest me before thy face for ever."
explanation: David is granted eternal, intimate communion: upheld in moral integrity and stationed perpetually before God's smiling face ('settest me before thy face for ever'). Psalm 41:12 (KJV) - "And as for me, thou upholdest me in mine integrity, and settest me before thy face for ever."

question: What grand doxology concludes Psalm 41 in verse 13, marking the end of Book 1 of the Psalter?
opt1: "The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended. Hallelujah, Amen;"
opt2: "Blessed be the LORD God of Israel from everlasting, and to everlasting. Amen, and Amen."
opt3: "Praise ye the Lord from the heavens: praise Him in the heights. Amen, and Amen;"
opt4: "The Lord reigneth forever: let all the tribes of Jacob shout for joy. Amen;"
correct: "Blessed be the LORD God of Israel from everlasting, and to everlasting. Amen, and Amen."
explanation: The majestic formal benediction terminating Book 1 (Psalms 1 to 41) of the five-book Psalter: praising Yahweh God of Israel from eternity to eternity, sealed with a double 'Amen'. Psalm 41:13 (KJV) - "Blessed be the LORD God of Israel from everlasting, and to everlasting. Amen, and Amen."

question: What is the Middle Eastern cultural significance of 'lifting up the heel' in Psalm 41:9?
opt1: Marching away into battle as a loyal general of the royal guard
opt2: Running swiftly like a courier to deliver glad tidings to the city
opt3: Showing the sole of the foot or kicking, representing extreme contempt, insubordination, and brutal betrayal after sacred table hospitality
opt4: Dancing before the ark of the covenant during harvest celebrations
correct: Showing the sole of the foot or kicking, representing extreme contempt, insubordination, and brutal betrayal after sacred table hospitality
explanation: In Near Eastern culture, sharing bread forged an inviolable covenant of mutual protection; lifting up the heel (like a vicious horse kicking its master) represented the apex of treacherous contempt. Psalm 41:9 (KJV) - "Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me."

question: How many total books comprise the canonical Book of Psalms, and which book concludes with Psalm 41?
opt1: Three books, mirroring the Temple divisions; Psalm 41 concludes Book 1
opt2: Seven books, mirroring the days of creation; Psalm 41 concludes Book 2
opt3: Twelve books, mirroring the twelve tribes; Psalm 41 concludes Book 3
opt4: Five books, mirroring the Torah; Psalm 41 concludes Book 1
correct: Five books, mirroring the Torah; Psalm 41 concludes Book 1
explanation: The Psalter is divided into five distinct books (Book 1: Ps 1-41; Book 2: Ps 42-72; Book 3: Ps 73-89; Book 4: Ps 90-106; Book 5: Ps 107-150), each ending in a doxology. Psalm 41:13 (KJV) - "Blessed be the LORD God of Israel from everlasting, and to everlasting. Amen, and Amen."

question: What famous animal metaphor of parched spiritual thirst opens Psalm 42:1-2?
opt1: "As the young lion roareth in the wilderness for prey, so crieth my soul for thy salvation, O Lord;"
opt2: "As the eagle mounteth up toward the sun, so soareth my spirit into thy holy presence, O God;"
opt3: "As the sheep wandereth in the dry valley seeking green pasture, so longeth my heart for thy courts, O Lord;"
opt4: "As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God. My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God: when shall I come and appear before God?"
correct: "As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God. My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God: when shall I come and appear before God?"
explanation: Book 2 of the Psalter opens with the Sons of Korah: a deer ('hart') gasping for life-giving streams in a drought portrays the believer's desperate thirst for the living God. Psalm 42:1-2 (KJV) - "As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God. My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God: when shall I come and appear before God?"

question: What painful diet and persistent mockery did the exiled psalmist endure in Psalm 42:3?
opt1: "My tears have been my meat day and night, while they continually say unto me, Where is thy God?"
opt2: "I have eaten ashes like bread, while the heathen shout, Thy sanctuary is burned with fire;"
opt3: "Bitter wormwood hath been my drink, while the archers mock, The king of Judah is fallen;"
opt4: "I have fasted in sackcloth, while the Philistines boast, Dagon hath prevailed over the ark;"
correct: "My tears have been my meat day and night, while they continually say unto me, Where is thy God?"
explanation: Grief replaced food: tears were his continuous nourishment day and night, while taunting skeptics poured psychological acid on his faith by demanding, 'Where is thy God?' Psalm 42:3 (KJV) - "My tears have been my meat day and night, while they continually say unto me, Where is thy God?"

question: What nostalgic memories of past corporate worship stir the psalmist's soul in Psalm 42:4?
opt1: Marching with the ark into the battlefield, and shouting victory over the princes of Moab
opt2: Going with the multitude to the house of God with the voice of joy and praise, with a multitude that kept holyday
opt3: Watching the high priest sprinkle the blood of atonement on the mercy seat between the cherubim
opt4: Listening to David play upon the harp of ten strings during the dedication of the royal palace
correct: Going with the multitude to the house of God with the voice of joy and praise, with a multitude that kept holyday
explanation: Isolated in northern exile, he pours out his soul remembering the ecstatic festival processions he once led to the sanctuary with joyful crowds celebrating annual feasts. Psalm 42:4 (KJV) - "When I remember these things, I pour out my soul in me: for I had gone with the multitude, I went with them to the house of God, with the voice of joy and praise, with a multitude that kept holyday."

question: What internal self-interrogation and sermon to his own soul forms the famous refrain in Psalm 42:5 and 11?
opt1: "Why weepest thou in the dark, O my spirit? why tremblest thou before men? trust in the Almighty: for He will avenge thy cause;"
opt2: "Why hast thou forgotten the covenant, O my heart? why art thou afraid of the sword? arise and sing: for the Lord is thy shield;"
opt3: "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance."
opt4: "Why dost thou mourn in sackcloth, O my soul? why dost thou despair in exile? look unto Zion: for thy salvation draweth near;"
correct: "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance."
explanation: Biblical self-counsel: instead of listening to his depressed emotions, the psalmist talks to his soul, rebuking discouragement and anchoring his hope in God's smiling countenance. Psalm 42:5 (KJV) - "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance."

question: From what northern geographical locations does the exiled psalmist remember God in Psalm 42:6?
opt1: From the wilderness of Paran, and the red crags of Mount Seir, from the oasis of Kadesh
opt2: From the plains of Moab, and the high peak of Mount Nebo, from the valley of Shittim
opt3: From the coastline of Tyre, and the cedar forests of Lebanon, from the river Kishon
opt4: From the land of Jordan, and of the Hermonites, from the hill Mizar
correct: From the land of Jordan, and of the Hermonites, from the hill Mizar
explanation: Far from Jerusalem, stranded in the extreme northern headwaters of the Jordan near Mount Hermon and an obscure peak ('hill Mizar'), the exile meditates on God. Psalm 42:6 (KJV) - "O my God, my soul is cast down within me: therefore will I remember thee from the land of Jordan, and of the Hermonites, from the hill Mizar."

question: What roaring cascade imagery portrays overwhelming waves of sorrow in Psalm 42:7?
opt1: "Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me."
opt2: "The stormy wind bloweth across the desert: the sands of the waste have buried my footsteps;"
opt3: "The thunderbolt striketh the mountain rocks: the floods of the river have carried away my tent;"
opt4: "The abyss of the sea openeth her mouth: the great dragons of the deep compass my soul;"
correct: "Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me."
explanation: Listening to the roaring waterfalls and cataracts of upper Jordan, he feels one ocean of sorrow answering another ('deep calleth unto deep') with crushing waves breaking over him. Psalm 42:7 (KJV) - "Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me."

question: What round-the-clock comfort does the LORD command for the believer in Psalm 42:8?
opt1: "For the Lord will send His angels at sunrise, and His fiery pillar shall guide my steps in the dark;"
opt2: "Yet the LORD will command his lovingkindness in the daytime, and in the night his song shall be with me, and my prayer unto the God of my life."
opt3: "Because the Lord will multiply His blessings in the morning, and His peace shall guard my tent at midnight;"
opt4: "The Lord will feed my soul with hidden manna, and give me sweet sleep under the shadow of His wings;"
correct: "Yet the LORD will command his lovingkindness in the daytime, and in the night his song shall be with me, and my prayer unto the God of my life."
explanation: A 24-hour cycle of grace: God's covenant lovingkindness (hesed) is commissioned as a guard by day, while songs of praise and prayer comfort the soul by night. Psalm 42:8 (KJV) - "Yet the LORD will command his lovingkindness in the daytime, and in the night his song shall be with me, and my prayer unto the God of my life."

question: What cutting physical metaphor depicts the agony of hearing daily enemy taunts in Psalm 42:10?
opt1: "As with burning coals upon my head, my adversaries mock my tears;"
opt2: "As with poisoned darts in my heart, the ungodly pierce my soul;"
opt3: "As with a sword in my bones, mine enemies reproach me; while they say daily unto me, Where is thy God?"
opt4: "As with iron chains upon my limbs, the heathen drag me into darkness;"
correct: "As with a sword in my bones, mine enemies reproach me; while they say daily unto me, Where is thy God?"
explanation: The relentless question 'Where is thy God?' cuts through him with the excruciating, shattering pain of a cold steel sword piercing deep into his marrow bones. Psalm 42:10 (KJV) - "As with a sword in my bones, mine enemies reproach me; while they say daily unto me, Where is thy God?"

question: How does the final refrain in Psalm 42:11 expand upon the vision of God compared to verse 5?
opt1: It calls God "the rock of my salvation" (whereas verse 5 called Him "the shield of my head")
opt2: It calls God "the King of glory" (whereas verse 5 called Him "the Lord of hosts")
opt3: It calls God "my deliverer in battle" (whereas verse 5 called Him "my hiding place")
opt4: It calls God "the health of my countenance, and my God" (whereas verse 5 spoke of "the help of his countenance")
correct: It calls God "the health of my countenance, and my God" (whereas verse 5 spoke of "the help of his countenance")
explanation: A wonderful progression of faith: God's smiling countenance (v. 5) brings healing and radiance to the believer's own downturned face ('health of my countenance', v. 11). Psalm 42:11 (KJV) - "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God."

question: Who were the 'Sons of Korah' credited in the superscription of Psalm 42?
opt1: A guild of Levitical musicians and temple gatekeepers descending from Korah, spared by sovereign grace when Korah rebelled (Num 26:11)
opt2: The sons of Saul who survived the battle of Mount Gilboa and joined David at Ziklag
opt3: A clan of Edomite sages who converted to the worship of Yahweh during David's reign
opt4: The descendants of Eli the high priest who were deposed from the altar at Shiloh
correct: A guild of Levitical musicians and temple gatekeepers descending from Korah, spared by sovereign grace when Korah rebelled (Num 26:11)
explanation: A monument of sovereign grace: though Korah died in rebellion (Num 16), his children were spared (Num 26:11) and became prominent composers and choir leaders in the tabernacle. Psalm 42:Title (KJV) - "To the chief Musician, Maschil, for the sons of Korah."

question: What judicial appeal and deliverances does the psalmist plead before God in Psalm 43:1?
opt1: "Judge me, O God, and plead my cause against an ungodly nation: O deliver me from the deceitful and unjust man."
opt2: "Avenge me, O Lord, and bring down fire upon the heathen: O break the teeth of the unrighteous ruler;"
opt3: "Hearken unto my cry, O Lord, and deliver my soul from the sword: O preserve me from the snares of death;"
opt4: "Save me, O God, and scatter the armies of the aliens: O hide me under the shadow of thy wings;"
correct: "Judge me, O God, and plead my cause against an ungodly nation: O deliver me from the deceitful and unjust man."
explanation: David commits his case to the supreme court of heaven, asking God to act as both Judge and Advocate against an ungodly collective and treacherous individual oppressors. Psalm 43:1 (KJV) - "Judge me, O God, and plead my cause against an ungodly nation: O deliver me from the deceitful and unjust man."

question: How does the psalmist address God while lamenting perceived abandonment and enemy oppression in Psalm 43:2?
opt1: "For thou art my rock and shield: why hast thou forsaken me? why do I wander in darkness without a lamp?"
opt2: "For thou art the God of my strength: why dost thou cast me off? why go I mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?"
opt3: "For thou art the horn of my salvation: why dost thou hide thy face? why am I troubled by the voice of the proud?"
opt4: "For thou art the portion of mine inheritance: why dost thou sleep? why am I trampled under the feet of strangers;"
correct: "For thou art the God of my strength: why dost thou cast me off? why go I mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?"
explanation: Even in perplexed agony, faith confesses God as the sole fortress and source of dynamic strength (Elohei Ma'uzzi). Psalm 43:2 (KJV) - "For thou art the God of my strength: why dost thou cast me off? why go I mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?"

question: Which two divine emissaries does the psalmist pray will lead him back to God's presence in Psalm 43:3?
opt1: "O send out thy mercy and thy lovingkindness: let them guide me; let them bring me into the courts of thy house;"
opt2: "O send out thy righteousness and thy peace: let them protect me; let them lead me to the city of the great King;"
opt3: "O send out thy light and thy truth: let them lead me; let them bring me unto thy holy hill, and to thy tabernacles."
opt4: "O send out thy power and thy glory: let them defend me; let them bring me unto thine holy sanctuary;"
correct: "O send out thy light and thy truth: let them lead me; let them bring me unto thy holy hill, and to thy tabernacles."
explanation: Light (illumination of God's presence) and Truth (covenant fidelity) are personified as heavenly guides escorting the exiled soul safely back to Mount Zion. Psalm 43:3 (KJV) - "O send out thy light and thy truth: let them lead me; let them bring me unto thy holy hill, and to thy tabernacles."

question: How does the psalmist describe God and express his worship upon reaching the altar in Psalm 43:4?
opt1: "Then will I offer burnt sacrifices with rejoicing: yea, with the trumpet will I exalt thee, O Lord of hosts;"
opt2: "Then will I bow before the holy ark in fear: yea, upon the psaltery will I magnify thy holy name;"
opt3: "Then will I pay my vows in the congregation: yea, with stringed instruments will I bless the King of glory;"
opt4: "Then will I go unto the altar of God, unto God my exceeding joy: yea, upon the harp will I praise thee, O God my God."
correct: "Then will I go unto the altar of God, unto God my exceeding joy: yea, upon the harp will I praise thee, O God my God."
explanation: God is not merely the giver of joy, but Joy Himself - the gladness of the soul's exultation, worshipped with the melody of the sacred harp. Psalm 43:4 (KJV) - "Then will I go unto the altar of God, unto God my exceeding joy: yea, upon the harp will I praise thee, O God my God."

question: What self-interrogation and concluding confession of hope completes the refrain in Psalm 43:5?
opt1: "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God."
opt2: "Why weepest thou, O my soul? and why art thou sore broken? wait upon the Lord: for he will wipe away all tears from mine eyes;"
opt3: "Why art thou fearful, O my soul? and why dost thou tremble? trust in the Almighty: for he is my high tower and my shield;"
opt4: "Why faintest thou, O my soul? and why dost thou complain? look unto the heavens: for the Lord shall deliver thee from death;"
correct: "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God."
explanation: The psalmist commands his disquieted soul to anchor its hope in God, who restores glowing radiance to the believer's countenance. Psalm 43:5 (KJV) - "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God."

question: To what sacred destination do the envoy guides of light and truth bring the psalmist in Psalm 43:3?
opt1: "unto the rivers of Babylon, and to the gates of Zion"
opt2: "unto thy holy hill, and to thy tabernacles"
opt3: "unto the garden of God, and to the living waters"
opt4: "unto the rock of Horeb, and to the tent of meeting"
correct: "unto thy holy hill, and to thy tabernacles"
explanation: Mount Zion ('thy holy hill') and the dwelling places of Yahweh ('thy tabernacles') represent the summit of covenant fellowship. Psalm 43:3 (KJV) - "O send out thy light and thy truth: let them lead me; let them bring me unto thy holy hill, and to thy tabernacles."

question: What unique structural and liturgical relationship links Psalm 43 to Psalm 42 in biblical scholarship?
opt1: Psalm 43 was written by Moses in the wilderness to conclude the Book of Exodus
opt2: Psalm 43 is the only Psalm entirely composed in the Aramaic language
opt3: Psalm 43 has no superscription and shares the identical threefold refrain with Psalm 42 (42:5, 42:11, 43:5), showing they originally formed one continuous lament poem
opt4: Psalm 43 was originally the preface to David's coronation psalm (Psalm 110)
correct: Psalm 43 has no superscription and shares the identical threefold refrain with Psalm 42 (42:5, 42:11, 43:5), showing they originally formed one continuous lament poem
explanation: In many Hebrew manuscripts, Psalm 42 and Psalm 43 form a single composite psalm structured around three stanzas, each ending with the identical chorus. Psalm 43:5 (KJV) - "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God."

question: What Hebrew expression in Psalm 43:4 translates into English as 'God my exceeding joy'?
opt1: El Shaddai Shalom (God the peace of my shelter)
opt2: Yahweh Tsidkenu (The Lord our righteousness)
opt3: Jehovah Nissi (The Lord our victorious banner)
opt4: El Simchat Gili (God the gladness of my exultation)
correct: El Simchat Gili (God the gladness of my exultation)
explanation: El Simchat Gili captures the supreme beatitude of the believer: finding supreme, boundless bliss in the Person and presence of God Himself. Psalm 43:4 (KJV) - "Then will I go unto the altar of God, unto God my exceeding joy: yea, upon the harp will I praise thee, O God my God."

question: What specific characteristic describes the individual opponent from whom deliverance is sought in Psalm 43:1?
opt1: "the deceitful and unjust man"
opt2: "the violent and bloodthirsty tyrant"
opt3: "the proud and haughty ruler"
opt4: "the treacherous and blasphemous king"
correct: "the deceitful and unjust man"
explanation: David points out the treacherous nature of his adversary, marked by craftiness, deceit, and moral unrighteousness. Psalm 43:1 (KJV) - "Judge me, O God, and plead my cause against an ungodly nation: O deliver me from the deceitful and unjust man."

question: In Psalm 43:4, what instrument does David explicitly designate for offering his songs of praise unto God?
opt1: The silver trumpet (Hatzotzerah)
opt2: The harp (Hebrew Kinnor)
opt3: The loud cymbal (Tzeltzelim)
opt4: The ten-stringed lute (Asor)
correct: The harp (Hebrew Kinnor)
explanation: The kinnor (harp/lyre) was David's primary instrument of devotion, tuned to praise Yahweh at the sacred sanctuary. Psalm 43:4 (KJV) - "Then will I go unto the altar of God, unto God my exceeding joy: yea, upon the harp will I praise thee, O God my God."

question: How does the community of Israel begin its historical recollection of God's ancestral wonders in Psalm 44:1?
opt1: "Our eyes have seen thy wonders in Egypt, O Lord, and our fathers rejoiced at the Red Sea;"
opt2: "We have heard with our ears, O God, our fathers have told us, what work thou didst in their days, in the times of old."
opt3: "We have read in the scroll of the covenant, O God, how thou broughtest us through the dry desert;"
opt4: "The elders of our tribes have testified unto us, O God, of the great battles won in the days of Joshua;"
correct: "We have heard with our ears, O God, our fathers have told us, what work thou didst in their days, in the times of old."
explanation: Israel recounts the sacred oral tradition handed down faithfully across generations testifying to God's mighty conquests in antiquity. Psalm 44:1 (KJV) - "We have heard with our ears, O God, our fathers have told us, what work thou didst in their days, in the times of old."

question: Why did Israel conquer and possess Canaan according to the theological declaration of Psalm 44:3?
opt1: "For they were more valiant than the Amorites, and their warriors were trained in archery from youth;"
opt2: "Because their kings made covenants with the nations, and their chariots were multiplied by Pharaoh;"
opt3: "For they got not the land in possession by their own sword, neither did their own arm save them: but thy right hand, and thine arm, and the light of thy countenance, because thou hadst a favour unto them."
opt4: "For their captains fought without fear, and the walls of Jericho fell before the shouts of their host;"
correct: "For they got not the land in possession by their own sword, neither did their own arm save them: but thy right hand, and thine arm, and the light of thy countenance, because thou hadst a favour unto them."
explanation: Human weaponry and military prowess contributed nothing; the inheritance was solely the sovereign gift of God's arm, right hand, and gracious countenance. Psalm 44:3 (KJV) - "For they got not the land in possession by their own sword, neither did their own arm save them: but thy right hand, and thine arm, and the light of thy countenance, because thou hadst a favour unto them."

question: What military renunciation does the psalmist profess regarding his personal hope of victory in Psalm 44:6?
opt1: "For I rely not upon horses, neither shall my iron shield deliver me;"
opt2: "For I lean not on captains of thousands, neither will chariots protect my head;"
opt3: "For I take no confidence in strong towers, neither shall the spear defend me;"
opt4: "For I will not trust in my bow, neither shall my sword save me."
correct: "For I will not trust in my bow, neither shall my sword save me."
explanation: True biblical faith abandons all self-reliance and carnal weapons, knowing salvation comes from Yahweh alone. Psalm 44:6 (KJV) - "For I will not trust in my bow, neither shall my sword save me."

question: What helpless slaughterhouse metaphor describes the suffering and dispersion of God's people in Psalm 44:11?
opt1: "Thou hast given us like sheep appointed for meat; and hast scattered us among the heathen."
opt2: "Thou hast delivered us like wild beasts into the hunter's net; and broken our bones in the wilderness;"
opt3: "Thou hast sold us like captives in the market of Egypt; and bound us in chains of brass;"
opt4: "Thou hast left us like birds caught in the fowler's snare; and plucked our feathers in the wind;"
correct: "Thou hast given us like sheep appointed for meat; and hast scattered us among the heathen."
explanation: The nation bewails being treated not as cherished covenant sons, but as livestock marked for slaughter and scattered among pagan nations. Psalm 44:11 (KJV) - "Thou hast given us like sheep appointed for meat; and hast scattered us among the heathen."

question: What striking commercial metaphor does the psalmist use in Psalm 44:12 to describe God relinquishing His people to their foes?
opt1: "Thou barterest thy heritage for silver, and exchangest thy sanctuary for heathen idols;"
opt2: "Thou sellest thy people for nought, and dost not increase thy wealth by their price."
opt3: "Thou hast mortgaged the land of promise, and left thy children without redemption;"
opt4: "Thou givest away thy portion for bread, and selleth the glory of Jacob to strangers;"
correct: "Thou sellest thy people for nought, and dost not increase thy wealth by their price."
explanation: The poet boldly laments that God surrendered them as if they held zero market value, gaining no profit from their captivity. Psalm 44:12 (KJV) - "Thou sellest thy people for nought, and dost not increase thy wealth by their price."

question: What remarkable claim of covenant loyalty does the nation maintain despite their profound humiliation in Psalm 44:17-18?
opt1: "Though we sinned against the law, yet did we offer our calves; and our priests ceased not to burn incense;"
opt2: "We have confessed our iniquities morning and evening; and turned away from the idols of Babylon;"
opt3: "All this is come upon us; yet have we not forgotten thee, neither have we dealt falsely in thy covenant. Our heart is not turned back, neither have our steps declined from thy way;"
opt4: "We built altars on every high hill; yet did we call upon the name of the Lord God of hosts;"
correct: "All this is come upon us; yet have we not forgotten thee, neither have we dealt falsely in thy covenant. Our heart is not turned back, neither have our steps declined from thy way;"
explanation: Unlike the common paradigm where disaster follows apostasy, this lament highlights innocent, righteous suffering without covenant violation. Psalm 44:17-18 (KJV) - "All this is come upon us; yet have we not forgotten thee, neither have we dealt falsely in thy covenant. Our heart is not turned back, neither have our steps declined from thy way;"

question: What desolate and fearsome location of crushing affliction is described in Psalm 44:19?
opt1: "Though thou hast plunged us into the depths of the pit, and bound us in irons of iron;"
opt2: "Though thou hast abandoned us in the desert of Zin, and burned our tents with coals;"
opt3: "Though thou hast brought us into the snare of the hunter, and delivered us to wild lions;"
opt4: "Though thou hast sore broken us in the place of dragons, and covered us with the shadow of death."
correct: "Though thou hast sore broken us in the place of dragons, and covered us with the shadow of death."
explanation: The 'place of dragons' (tannim - jackals/sea-monsters/wilderness ruins) symbolizes utter desolation, darkness, and impending death. Psalm 44:19 (KJV) - "Though thou hast sore broken us in the place of dragons, and covered us with the shadow of death."

question: On what basis does the psalmist argue in Psalm 44:20-21 that secret idolatry cannot be hidden from God?
opt1: "Shall not God search this out? for he knoweth the secrets of the heart."
opt2: "For the eyes of the Lord run to and fro upon the mountains of Lebanon;"
opt3: "Because his ears hear every whisper spoken in the secret chambers of kings;"
opt4: "For no man can hide from the presence of the Almighty or dwell in darkness;"
correct: "Shall not God search this out? for he knoweth the secrets of the heart."
explanation: God's omniscient scrutiny searches the deepest hidden recesses of human intention and affections. Psalm 44:21 (KJV) - "Shall not God search this out? for he knoweth the secrets of the heart."

question: Which verse from Psalm 44:22 does the Apostle Paul famously quote in Romans 8:36 regarding Christian suffering and persecution?
opt1: "Through thee will we push down our enemies: through thy name will we tread them under;"
opt2: "Yea, for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter."
opt3: "Thou makest us a reproach to our neighbours, a scorn and a derision to them that are round about us;"
opt4: "Awake, why sleepest thou, O Lord? arise, cast us not off for ever;"
correct: "Yea, for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter."
explanation: Paul cites this verse in Romans 8:36 to establish that covenant saints endure suffering precisely 'for thy sake', yet remain more than conquerors in Christ. Psalm 44:22 (KJV) - "Yea, for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter."

question: What passionate concluding petition calls God to awaken and redeem His people in Psalm 44:23 and 44:26?
opt1: "Hearken, O Lord of hosts, and avenge our blood: march through the heathen in thy wrath;"
opt2: "Remember the oath made unto Abraham, O God: blow the trumpet and gather thy scattered sheep;"
opt3: "Awake, why sleepest thou, O Lord? arise, cast us not off for ever ... Arise for our help, and redeem us for thy mercies' sake."
opt4: "Open thine eyes, O King of Israel: shatter the bows of the Philistines and build Zion;"
correct: "Awake, why sleepest thou, O Lord? arise, cast us not off for ever ... Arise for our help, and redeem us for thy mercies' sake."
explanation: The psalm ends not with bitter resentment, but with a daring anthropomorphic cry for God to arise and redeem His people for the sake of His steadfast covenant mercies (hesed). Psalm 44:23, 26 (KJV) - "Awake, why sleepest thou, O Lord? arise, cast us not off for ever ... Arise for our help, and redeem us for thy mercies' sake."

question: How does the poet introduce his inspired royal wedding composition in Psalm 45:1?
opt1: "My soul is lifted up with sacred music: I sing of the beauty of the daughter of Zion: my mouth overflows with poetry;"
opt2: "The spirit of the Lord is upon me to declare glad tidings: my words are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb;"
opt3: "My heart is inditing a good matter: I speak of the things which I have made touching the king: my tongue is the pen of a ready writer."
opt4: "Hearken, ye princes, to the wisdom of my mouth: I utter a song of great joy concerning the house of David;"
correct: "My heart is inditing a good matter: I speak of the things which I have made touching the king: my tongue is the pen of a ready writer."
explanation: The Hebrew verb rachash ('inditing') means boiling or bubbling over; the poet's enthusiastic devotion to the King makes his tongue swift as the reed-pen of a skilled scribe. Psalm 45:1 (KJV) - "My heart is inditing a good matter: I speak of the things which I have made touching the king: my tongue is the pen of a ready writer."

question: What radiant portrait of the King's personal grace and speech is presented in Psalm 45:2?
opt1: "Thou art taller than all the sons of Israel: wisdom shineth upon thy brow: therefore the kings bring tribute;"
opt2: "Thou art mightier than the cedars of Lebanon: victory is in thy right hand: therefore the nations bow before thee;"
opt3: "Thou art crowned with pure gold from Ophir: righteousness floweth from thy throne: therefore thy fame shall endure;"
opt4: "Thou art fairer than the children of men: grace is poured into thy lips: therefore God hath blessed thee for ever."
correct: "Thou art fairer than the children of men: grace is poured into thy lips: therefore God hath blessed thee for ever."
explanation: Christ, the ultimate Messianic King, surpasses all fallen mortals in transcendent moral beauty and gracious speech (Luke 4:22). Psalm 45:2 (KJV) - "Thou art fairer than the children of men: grace is poured into thy lips: therefore God hath blessed thee for ever."

question: For what threefold ethical cause does the warrior King ride forth prosperously in Psalm 45:4?
opt1: "because of truth and meekness and righteousness"
opt2: "because of power and majesty and dominion"
opt3: "because of judgment and vengeance and glory"
opt4: "because of wealth and empire and conquest"
correct: "because of truth and meekness and righteousness"
explanation: Unlike carnal conquerors driven by vain ambition, the Messianic King wages war purely to establish truth, gentle meekness, and holy righteousness. Psalm 45:4 (KJV) - "And in thy majesty ride prosperously because of truth and meekness and righteousness; and thy right hand shall teach thee terrible things."

question: What profound declaration of the King's deity and eternal sceptre in Psalm 45:6 is quoted in Hebrews 1:8?
opt1: "Thy kingdom, O Lord, is an everlasting kingdom: thy dominion endureth throughout all ages;"
opt2: "Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: the sceptre of thy kingdom is a right sceptre."
opt3: "Thy sanctuary, O God, is holy from generation to generation: the crown of thy head shall never fade;"
opt4: "Thou rulest, O Most High, over heaven and earth: the rod of thy power is an iron rod;"
correct: "Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: the sceptre of thy kingdom is a right sceptre."
explanation: The King is directly addressed as God (Elohim) whose throne is eternal, applied directly to the Son in Hebrews 1:8 as undeniable proof of Christ's divinity. Psalm 45:6 (KJV) - "Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: the sceptre of thy kingdom is a right sceptre."

question: Why has God anointed the King with the oil of gladness above His fellows in Psalm 45:7?
opt1: "Thou offeredst thousands of rams and ten thousands of rivers of oil: therefore God hath set thee upon Zion;"
opt2: "Thou destroyedst the ungodly with an iron rod: therefore the Lord hath given thee the kingdoms of the world;"
opt3: "Thou lovest righteousness, and hatest wickedness: therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows."
opt4: "Thou walkedst in the statutes of Moses without spot: therefore the Almighty hath multiplied thy seed;"
correct: "Thou lovest righteousness, and hatest wickedness: therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows."
explanation: The King's supreme coronation and joyful anointing stem from His absolute love for righteousness and holy hatred of iniquity (quoted in Hebrews 1:9). Psalm 45:7 (KJV) - "Thou lovest righteousness, and hatest wickedness: therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows."

question: Which three exotic spices perfume the King's royal garments out of the ivory palaces in Psalm 45:8?
opt1: "frankincense, and spikenard, and cinnamon"
opt2: "calamus, and saffron, and cedar"
opt3: "sweet cane, and stacte, and onycha"
opt4: "myrrh, and aloes, and cassia"
correct: "myrrh, and aloes, and cassia"
explanation: Myrrh (bitter suffering and burial), aloes (royal healing), and cassia (deep fragrant devotion) waft from the ivory palaces, gladdening the King. Psalm 45:8 (KJV) - "All thy garments smell of myrrh, and aloes, and cassia, out of the ivory palaces, whereby they have made thee glad."

question: Who stands at the King's right hand adorned in the finest gold of Ophir in Psalm 45:9?
opt1: "the queen in gold of Ophir"
opt2: "the high priest in the breastplate of Urim"
opt3: "the captain of the host in golden armor"
opt4: "the daughter of Tyre with her bridal crown"
correct: "the queen in gold of Ophir"
explanation: The Queen consort, typifying the Church of the redeemed, stands at the place of ultimate honor at the King's right hand in pure gold of Ophir. Psalm 45:9 (KJV) - "Kings' daughters were among thy honourable women: upon thy right hand did stand the queen in gold of Ophir."

question: What total break with the past is commanded of the royal bride in Psalm 45:10?
opt1: "Depart, O bride, from the land of Egypt; and remember no more the idols of the heathen;"
opt2: "Hearken, O daughter, and consider, and incline thine ear; forget also thine own people, and thy father's house;"
opt3: "Leave behind thy silver and thy gold; and follow the ark of the covenant into the sanctuary;"
opt4: "Wash thy hands in innocency, O maiden; and cease from mourning for the sorrows of the past;"
correct: "Hearken, O daughter, and consider, and incline thine ear; forget also thine own people, and thy father's house;"
explanation: True union with the King requires wholehearted renunciation of prior allegiances and former earthly family connections. Psalm 45:10 (KJV) - "Hearken, O daughter, and consider, and incline thine ear; forget also thine own people, and thy father's house;"

question: How is the beauty and magnificent bridal attire of the King's daughter described in Psalm 45:13-14?
opt1: "The bride of the king is adorned with pearls from the eastern sea: her veil is woven of fine linen of Egypt;"
opt2: "The queen is clothed in purple from Tyre: her neck is encircled with rubies and sapphires from the mountains;"
opt3: "The king's daughter is all glorious within: her clothing is of wrought gold. She shall be brought unto the king in raiment of needlework: the virgins her companions that follow her shall be brought unto thee."
opt4: "The daughter of Zion is covered in scarlet: her robes are embroidered with silver thread and lilies of the valley;"
correct: "The king's daughter is all glorious within: her clothing is of wrought gold. She shall be brought unto the king in raiment of needlework: the virgins her companions that follow her shall be brought unto thee."
explanation: Her inward character matches her outward majesty: clothing of gold filigree and intricately woven needlework, accompanied by pure virgin companions. Psalm 45:13-14 (KJV) - "The king's daughter is all glorious within: her clothing is of wrought gold. She shall be brought unto the king in raiment of needlework: the virgins her companions that follow her shall be brought unto thee."

question: What dynastic promise regarding offspring and universal dominion concludes Psalm 45:16?
opt1: "Thy sons shall inherit the throne of David, and thy daughters shall build houses in Jerusalem;"
opt2: "Thy seed shall be multiplied like the stars of heaven, and possess the gates of their enemies;"
opt3: "Out of thy loins shall come priests and prophets, who shall govern the nations in peace;"
opt4: "Instead of thy fathers shall be thy children, whom thou mayest make princes in all the earth."
correct: "Instead of thy fathers shall be thy children, whom thou mayest make princes in all the earth."
explanation: The bride loses her ancestral father's house but gains a worldwide spiritual progeny: children appointed as princes across all the earth. Psalm 45:16 (KJV) - "Instead of thy fathers shall be thy children, whom thou mayest make princes in all the earth."

question: What majestic three-part opening confession of divine security begins Psalm 46:1?
opt1: "The Lord is my shepherd and shield, an ever-living rock in the storm;"
opt2: "The Almighty is our tower of safety, a swift deliverer in the day of battle;"
opt3: "God is our light and salvation, a mighty fortress against the adversary;"
opt4: "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble."
correct: "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble."
explanation: This verse formed the foundation for Martin Luther's famous Reformation anthem 'Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott' ('A Mighty Fortress Is Our God'). Psalm 46:1 (KJV) - "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble."

question: What catastrophic natural convulsions will not terrify the people of God according to Psalm 46:2-3?
opt1: "though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea; Though the waters thereof roar and be troubled, though the mountains shake with the swelling thereof."
opt2: "though the sun be darkened, and though the stars fall from the firmament like withered figs;"
opt3: "though great earthquakes tear down the cities, and locusts consume every green thing;"
opt4: "though plagues destroy ten thousand at our side, and lightning consume the high cedars;"
correct: "though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea; Though the waters thereof roar and be troubled, though the mountains shake with the swelling thereof."
explanation: Even if creation itself undergoes total de-creation - earth displaced and mountains crashing into ocean depths - faith remains unshakable in God. Psalm 46:2-3 (KJV) - "Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea; Though the waters thereof roar and be troubled, though the mountains shake with the swelling thereof. Selah."

question: What serene contrast to the roaring oceans brings joy to God's dwelling place in Psalm 46:4?
opt1: "There is a fountain of living water flowing from the threshold of the sanctuary;"
opt2: "There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God, the holy place of the tabernacles of the most High."
opt3: "There is a well of salvation dug in the midst of Zion by the kings of Judah;"
opt4: "There is a stream of milk and honey refreshing the courts of the Lord of hosts;"
correct: "There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God, the holy place of the tabernacles of the most High."
explanation: While worldly powers are like violent oceanic deluges, God's presence is a quiet, continuous river of grace gladdening the City of God. Psalm 46:4 (KJV) - "There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God, the holy place of the tabernacles of the most High."

question: Why will the city of God remain immovable, and when will God intervene to help her according to Psalm 46:5?
opt1: "Her walls are made of solid rock; she cannot fall: God shall defend her at midnight;"
opt2: "The ark of the covenant rests in her temple: God will preserve her before the sun goes down;"
opt3: "God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved: God shall help her, and that right early."
opt4: "Ten thousand angels camp around her gates: God shall deliver her in the noon hour;"
correct: "God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved: God shall help her, and that right early."
explanation: The security of the church rests entirely on the indwelling presence of God, whose timely help arrives at the break of dawn ('right early'). Psalm 46:5 (KJV) - "God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved: God shall help her, and that right early."

question: What happens when earthly nations rage and God utters His voice in Psalm 46:6?
opt1: "The kings assembled their hosts: he blew with his breath, and they perished like stubble;"
opt2: "The pagan empires clashed in fury: he stretched forth his arm, and their crowns were broken;"
opt3: "The nations set their battle in array: he sent his thunderbolts, and their chariots sank into the sea;"
opt4: "The heathen raged, the kingdoms were moved: he uttered his voice, the earth melted."
correct: "The heathen raged, the kingdoms were moved: he uttered his voice, the earth melted."
explanation: A single spoken syllable from Yahweh instantly dissolves all roaring human empires and melts the physical earth into submission. Psalm 46:6 (KJV) - "The heathen raged, the kingdoms were moved: he uttered his voice, the earth melted."

question: What repeated two-line refrain serves as the fortress chorus in Psalm 46:7 and 46:11?
opt1: "The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our refuge. Selah."
opt2: "The Holy One of Israel reigns; the rock of ages is our defense. Selah."
opt3: "The King of kings fights for his people; the shield of Abraham is our salvation. Selah."
opt4: "The Lord God omnipotent reigneth; the horn of David is our deliverer. Selah."
correct: "The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our refuge. Selah."
explanation: Yahweh Sabaoth (Lord of armadas/armies) is on our side, and the covenant God of Jacob is our unassailable high tower (misgav). Psalm 46:7, 11 (KJV) - "The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our refuge. Selah."

question: What invitation is extended to believers to observe the sovereign acts of Yahweh in Psalm 46:8?
opt1: "Look up, and see the wonders of the Most High, how he planteth righteousness in Zion;"
opt2: "Come, behold the works of the LORD, what desolations he hath made in the earth."
opt3: "Enter into his gates, and consider his judgments, how he overthroweth the wicked in the pit;"
opt4: "Draw near, ye tribes of Israel, and behold how his glory covereth the mountain;"
correct: "Come, behold the works of the LORD, what desolations he hath made in the earth."
explanation: The faithful are summoned to survey God's righteous judgments and the ruin He brings upon proud warring empires. Psalm 46:8 (KJV) - "Come, behold the works of the LORD, what desolations he hath made in the earth."

question: What three instruments of warfare does God destroy to bring universal peace in Psalm 46:9?
opt1: He shatters the iron sword, breaks the bronze helmet, and drowns the warhorse in the sea
opt2: He bends the iron javelin, destroys the siege engine, and tramples the shields under foot
opt3: He breaketh the bow, cutteth the spear in sunder, and burneth the chariot in the fire
opt4: He snaps the oak staff, burns the archer's quiver, and dissolves the chain mail in furnace heat
correct: He breaketh the bow, cutteth the spear in sunder, and burneth the chariot in the fire
explanation: God completely disarms global militarism by breaking bows, snapping spears in two, and incinerating war chariots. Psalm 46:9 (KJV) - "He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder; he burneth the chariot in the fire."

question: What sovereign divine command silences all human strivings in Psalm 46:10?
opt1: "Stand fast, and watch the salvation of the Lord: for the battle is not yours, but God's;"
opt2: "Fear not, little flock, for it is the Father's good pleasure to give you the everlasting kingdom;"
opt3: "Rest in the Lord, and wait patiently for him: for he will establish peace unto the ends of the world;"
opt4: "Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth."
correct: "Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth."
explanation: The Hebrew verb harpu ('Be still') means 'let go, cease striving, drop your hands'; human panic must give way to reverent submission before God's supreme majesty. Psalm 46:10 (KJV) - "Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth."

question: What is the musical designation 'upon Alamoth' in the superscription of Psalm 46 generally understood to mean?
opt1: Set to soprano or maiden voices (from the Hebrew 'almah', maiden or virgin), indicating a high-pitched choral register
opt2: Played exclusively upon eight-stringed harps imported from Egypt
opt3: A funeral dirge chanted only on the Day of Atonement
opt4: A marching rhythm beaten upon large bronze war drums
correct: Set to soprano or maiden voices (from the Hebrew 'almah', maiden or virgin), indicating a high-pitched choral register
explanation: 'Alamoth' (plural of almah, virgin/young woman) indicates music scored for treble or high soprano voices, creating an uplifting, triumphant tone. Psalm 46:Title (KJV) - "To the chief Musician for the sons of Korah, A Song upon Alamoth."

question: What worldwide physical and vocal celebration opens Psalm 47:1?
opt1: "O clap your hands, all ye people; shout unto God with the voice of triumph."
opt2: "O sound the trumpet in Zion, all ye tribes; sing unto the Lord with thanksgiving and joy;"
opt3: "O bow your heads, all ye nations; worship the Holy One of Israel in solemn silence;"
opt4: "O lift up your banners, all ye lands; rejoice before the King with harps and cymbals;"
correct: "O clap your hands, all ye people; shout unto God with the voice of triumph."
explanation: The call to applaud and shout aloud with joyful triumph is universal, embracing all ethnic peoples of the earth in Yahweh's kingdom. Psalm 47:1 (KJV) - "O clap your hands, all ye people; shout unto God with the voice of triumph."

question: What two awesome titles are ascribed to God as the reason for this universal celebration in Psalm 47:2?
opt1: "For the Lord of hosts is mighty; he is the creator of the ends of the world;"
opt2: "For the LORD most high is terrible; he is a great King over all the earth."
opt3: "For the Holy One of Jacob is righteous; he is the supreme judge over all nations;"
opt4: "For the Almighty is glorious in power; he is an everlasting rock of salvation;"
correct: "For the LORD most high is terrible; he is a great King over all the earth."
explanation: Yahweh Elyon is 'terrible' (awe-inspiring, fearsome in majestic holiness) and the cosmic Sovereign over all terrestrial kingdoms. Psalm 47:2 (KJV) - "For the LORD most high is terrible; he is a great King over all the earth."

question: What promise of global submission under God's people is articulated in Psalm 47:3?
opt1: "He shall scatter the ungodly like chaff, and destroy their idols in the fire;"
opt2: "He shall break their iron chariots, and give their palaces to the righteous for a prey;"
opt3: "He shall subdue the people under us, and the nations under our feet."
opt4: "He shall deliver their captains into our hand, and make their strong cities desolate;"
correct: "He shall subdue the people under us, and the nations under our feet."
explanation: God subjugates rival kingdoms, placing the nations under the spiritual dominion of the covenant community. Psalm 47:3 (KJV) - "He shall subdue the people under us, and the nations under our feet."

question: How does the psalmist describe the promised land and covenant heritage in Psalm 47:4?
opt1: "He shall give us the garden of pleasure, the mountain of Moriah where Abraham worshipped. Selah."
opt2: "He shall establish our borders from the Euphrates to the sea, the land flowing with milk and honey. Selah."
opt3: "He shall appoint our dwelling in safety, the holy city of David his chosen servant. Selah."
opt4: "He shall choose our inheritance for us, the excellency of Jacob whom he loved. Selah."
correct: "He shall choose our inheritance for us, the excellency of Jacob whom he loved. Selah."
explanation: The inheritance of the saints is not self-selected but chosen by God's sovereign grace, named 'the excellency [glory/pride] of Jacob whom he loved'. Psalm 47:4 (KJV) - "He shall choose our inheritance for us, the excellency of Jacob whom he loved. Selah."

question: What prophetic depiction of divine ascension with royal fanfare is portrayed in Psalm 47:5?
opt1: "God is gone up with a shout, the LORD with the sound of a trumpet."
opt2: "The King hath entered his sanctuary with rejoicing, the Lord with the voice of the archangel;"
opt3: "The Lord hath ascended the holy hill of Zion, the Almighty with stringed instruments;"
opt4: "God hath taken his seat upon the cherubim, the Holy One with the blowing of the ram's horn;"
correct: "God is gone up with a shout, the LORD with the sound of a trumpet."
explanation: Historically reflecting the Ark's procession up Mount Zion, this verse prophetically prefigures Christ's triumphant ascension into heaven. Psalm 47:5 (KJV) - "God is gone up with a shout, the LORD with the sound of a trumpet."

question: What enthusiastic quadruple exhortation to worship God our King is recorded in Psalm 47:6?
opt1: "Give thanks unto the Lord, give thanks: bless his holy name, bless him for ever;"
opt2: "Sing praises to God, sing praises: sing praises unto our King, sing praises."
opt3: "Exalt the Lord our God, exalt him: bow down at his footstool, worship in holiness;"
opt4: "Rejoice in the Lord, rejoice: proclaim his great salvation, declare his glory;"
correct: "Sing praises to God, sing praises: sing praises unto our King, sing praises."
explanation: Four rapid-fire commands to 'sing praises' (zammeru) highlight the boundless delight and repetitive fervor due to our divine King. Psalm 47:6 (KJV) - "Sing praises to God, sing praises: sing praises unto our King, sing praises."

question: With what specific spiritual quality must praise be offered to God as King of all the earth in Psalm 47:7?
opt1: "sing ye praises with loud instruments"
opt2: "sing ye praises with clean hands"
opt3: "sing ye praises with understanding"
opt4: "sing ye praises with dancing and timbrels"
correct: "sing ye praises with understanding"
explanation: Biblical worship is not blind emotionalism but intelligent adoration based on doctrinal truth (Hebrew Maskil). Psalm 47:7 (KJV) - "For God is the King of all the earth: sing ye praises with understanding."

question: Where does God sit as He exercises His sovereign dominion over the heathen in Psalm 47:8?
opt1: "God ruleth over the nations: God sitteth between the cherubim of the sanctuary;"
opt2: "God judgeth the Gentiles: God sitteth upon the circle of the earth in power;"
opt3: "God conquereth the pagan lands: God sitteth on the mountain of his congregation;"
opt4: "God reigneth over the heathen: God sitteth upon the throne of his holiness."
correct: "God reigneth over the heathen: God sitteth upon the throne of his holiness."
explanation: God's global throne is defined primarily by absolute holiness; moral purity characterizes His eternal sovereignty. Psalm 47:8 (KJV) - "God reigneth over the heathen: God sitteth upon the throne of his holiness."

question: How are the converted Gentile rulers described, and to whom do the 'shields of the earth' belong in Psalm 47:9?
opt1: "The princes of the people are gathered together, even the people of the God of Abraham: for the shields of the earth belong unto God: he is greatly exalted."
opt2: "The kings of the nations fall down in sackcloth before the ark: for the crowns of the world belong to the Son of David;"
